F: What he's going to say?
M: He saw it.

F: Did you talk to him?
M: No.  I figured I'd just let it wait.
F: Cried hard?
M: Yeah, I could hear him crying through the floorboards in my room.
F: [BREATHING]
F: What is he doing out here at that hour?
M: I don't know.
F: He's dreaming about him again, walking the streets.
M: I guess he is.
M: I don't know the meaning of it.  But I know we've made terrible mistake with father.
F: What do you mean a mistake?
M: I just--why shouldn't he walk the nights waiting for him, huh?  Do we contradict him do we say we don't have any hope any more that he's not coming back?
F: What do you want to do, argue with him?
M: I don't want to argue with him, it's just for God's sake it's time he realized that no one believes with him any more.
M: I got to.
F: What, can you prove it?  What proof do you have?  Can you prove it?
M: For God's sake, three years?  Nobody comes back after three years. It's insane.
F: To you it is, to me it is.  But to your father?  You can talk yourself 'til you're blue in the face but there's was no grave and there is no body.  So where are you?

F: The trouble is those god damn news papers.  Every month some boy comes back missing longer then Larry so--

F: Well, that's only your business, Chris.

F: Well, what do you want me to do?  You're old enough known your own business.

F: I'm just saying.

M: She is not Larry's girl.
F: From father's point of view he is not dead and you have no right to take his girl.  I'm just saying that you can go on from there if you know where to go but I'm saying I don't know where to go.  See, I don't know.
M: I don't know why it is you know every time I reach out for something I have to pull back 'cause I'm afraid it's going to hurt somebody.  All my life...
F: You're a considerate fellow.  There's nothing wrong in that.
M: To hell with that.
F: Did you ask Annie yet?
M: No, I wanted to get this all sorted out first.
F: Well, how do you know she's going to marry you?  Maybe she feels same way your father does.
F: The trouble is you don't see enough women, you never did.
M: So what?  I'm just--I'm not fast with women.
F: I don't see why it has to be Annie.
M: Because it is.
F: That's a good answer but it doesn't answer anything.  You haven't seen her since you went away to war, it's been five years.
M: I don't know, it I think of her, I grew up next to her.  She is what I think of when I think of a wife.
F: He thinks he's coming back, Chris.  You marry that girl you're pronouncing him dead.
F: Do you know what that'll do to you, to your father, do you know?  I don't.
